platforms.title: 3 Things That Make Trigger Finger More Likely
platforms.meta_description: A finger that catches or locks when you bend it isn't just from typing too much. Diabetes and repetitive gripping both raise the risk more than people expect.
platforms.body_html:
A finger that catches, clicks, or locks in a bent position before suddenly popping straight is usually trigger finger, medically known as stenosing tenosynovitis. The tendon that bends your finger runs through a narrow tunnel of tissue called the A1 pulley; when the tendon develops a small nodule or the pulley thickens from repeated friction, the tendon catches every time it tries to slide through, especially first thing in the morning when everything is stiffer. It's uncomfortable and sometimes alarming the first few times it happens, but it's rarely dangerous — and it's also more common, and more treatable, than most people assume.

Three Things That Raise Your Risk

First, diabetes. People with diabetes develop trigger finger at a notably higher rate than the general population, likely related to how elevated blood sugar affects collagen in tendons over time — this is one of the most consistently reported associations in hand surgery literature. Second, repetitive gripping: jobs and hobbies involving a lot of forceful gripping, like manual labor, cooking, or racket sports, put sustained friction on that same spot in the tendon sheath. Third, sex and age — trigger finger is more common in women, and risk rises through midlife. None of these alone guarantees you'll develop it, but stacking more than one raises the odds meaningfully.

Swap Guesswork For What The Research Shows

Steroid injections are the standard first treatment, and a meta-analysis pooling six randomized controlled trials with 368 participants found that about 63.7% of steroid-injected fingers resolved successfully compared with 27.5% in the control groups — a meaningful difference, though the meta-analysis also noted that success rates varied depending on how severe the triggering was and how long people were followed up. A splint that keeps the finger straight overnight is a reasonable first step for milder cases and carries essentially no risk, though it works more slowly than an injection. If a finger still locks after one or two injections, or locks completely and won't straighten on its own, a short outpatient surgical release of the pulley is a well-established option with a high success rate. What doesn't help much is simply waiting it out and hoping the clicking stops — untreated trigger finger tends to plateau rather than resolve on its own, so getting it evaluated sooner rather than later tends to mean simpler treatment.

So the next time your finger catches on the way to a fist: is it just stiffness, or has it been doing this for weeks now? It's also worth looking at what happens between flare-ups, not just during treatment. Gentle tendon-gliding exercises — making a full fist, then a hook fist, then a straight hand, moving through each position slowly — can help keep the tendon moving smoothly through the pulley and are commonly recommended by hand therapists alongside splinting. Changing how you grip matters too: tools and utensils with thicker, padded handles spread the gripping force across the palm instead of concentrating it right where the pulley sits, which is a simple, low-cost change for anyone whose job or hobbies involve a lot of repetitive gripping. None of this guarantees prevention, especially if diabetes is part of the picture, but it lowers the mechanical load that makes triggering worse over time.
